newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - EMU is joker in pack for 1999 rate futures.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - EMU is joker in pack for 1999 rate futures.

text.p: The year will be 1999, the world interest rate picture will be benign, but euro markets will be a gamble.
So say analysts who are now starting to scan the economic horizons for clues on how to trade interest rate futures in the new world after the introduction of a single European currency.
Investors can look to low global interest rates in the next couple of years, but European economic and monetary Union (EMU) may yet alter the picture in Europe, they add.
"EMU is untried and untested," said Gerard Lyons, chief economist at DKB International in London.
"The risk is that the European Central Bank will be keen to make the euro a hard currency, and will raise rates more than it needs to."
If that is the case, it will buck the global interest rate trend, Lyons said.

"There is every scope that interest rates around the world will remain at low levels. The 1970s and the 1980s were the inflation years, and markets tend to be heavily influenced by the recent past. But this time, recovery will not bring inflation."
CURRENT ASSUMPTIONS

Market predictions for interest rates in 1999, the scheduled launch date for the single currency, are reflected in the interest rate futures strips, three-month interest rate futures listed out for several years.

They show moderately higher interest rates for Japan and the U.S. than currently. The LIFFE Euromark future, widely considered to be the likely benchmark for the euro interest rate future, also suggests a mild upward move in euro rates from current German levels.

The Eurodollar future listed in Chicago this week was anticipating U.S. money market rates of around 6.30 percent in March 1999, the first futures delivery month following an expected punctual start to EMU in January 1999.
U.S. federal funds are more than 75 basis points lower at 5.50 percent, after the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) left rates unchanged at its most recent meeting on July 2.
Nigel Richardson, head of bond research at Yamaichi International Europe in London, said futures market expectations of higher U.S. interest rates were overdone.
"U.S. rates will go up by 25-50 basis points and then start to come down by 100-150 basis points by the beginning of 1999."
U.S. interest rates will benefit from the U.S. economy's place in the cycle by 1999, analysts said.
"We may get a recession in the U.S. and liquidity conditions will be favourable," said Kirit Shah, bond strategist at Sanwa International in London.
But interest rates in the U.S. will remain higher than those in Japan and Europe, the futures strips suggest.

March 1999 Euroyen futures discounted money market rates of around 1.70 percent, more than a full point above current three-month deposit rates. The Official Discount Rate in Japan is 0.50 percent, and there is market talk of a rise in official rates before year-end.
"Japanese interest rates will be higher than they are now," said Lyons.
"They will be back towards 2.0-2.50 percent, returning to normality. But normality in the new interest rate regime will be relatively low."
CRACKS IN THE CRYSTAL BALL

Analysts attempting to predict interest rates for the euro have to battle with second guessing the mind-set of European central bankers meeting in groups, and also with calculating which countries will be in EMU's first wave.
Futures markets have got it wrong, economists say.

"It is very likely that Spain and Portugal will join EMU in the first wave and increasingly likely that Italy will do so, but that is not being reflected in the markets," said Ken Wattret, international economist at Paribas Capital Markets in London.
Interest rate contracts listed on futures exchanges in Britain, France and Spain suggest France and Germany will join EMU punctually in 1999, but Spain may not make it, and Italy will miss it.
French and German three-month interest rate futures show converging interest rates.

MATIF's PIBOR future and LIFFE's Euromark future are indicating French and German money market rates of around 4.15-4.25 percent for March 1999. The current official French intervention rate is 3.10 percent and Germany's discount rate is 2.50 percent.
But Italian interest rates, as seen in futures prices, remain out of alignment.

March 1999 Eurolire on LIFFE imply money market rates of around 5.35 percent, more than one percentage point above France and Germany, yet below the Italian discount rate, recently cut to 6.25 percent.

Spanish MIBOR futures listed on local exchange MEFF indicate interbank rates of around 4.80 percent in 1999, close to current official interest rates of 5.25 percent, but more than half a point away from the futures markets' perception of post-EMU rates.
But if the European Central Bank does resist the temptation to raise rates, futures market predictions of euro rates in 1999 could also be overstated, analysts said.

"Interest rates after EMU will be lower than the markets are showing if the Bundesbank persists in offering three percent repo rates," said Michael Derks, cross market fixed income specialist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in London. -- International Bonds Unit +44 171 542 6320
